subjects.displayTitle: The voice of Divinity: revelation, servitude and response
subjects.introduction: A man in prison says that the words leaving his lips are not his own, that a Spirit speaks within his breast, and in the same breath calls himself a servant of God. Bahá’u’lláh asks us to hold both together, then presses the question further: who was it that spoke on Sinai, the Tree or the One within the Tree, and why should that voice be welcomed in one age and refused in another? Moses hearing his name from a burning bush [1] and Jesus telling Philip that to see him is to see the Father [2] stand close by as kindred encounters. The Temple with its tongue and limbs, the Pen awaiting a command, the Book that calls its readers to life, each is a way of thinking about how the unseen reaches the seen. To listen well, one has to learn how the Manifestation stands in relation to God, how the Holy Spirit moves through a human frame, and what the stations of that one voice allow it to say. Hearing is answered in a life: in trustworthiness, friendship, wisdom and service.

order.why: Introduce the differing stations of speech and the equality of words in the divine purpose.

He is verily the Almighty, the All-Powerful. order.why: Restore the question about Sinai and the complete sequence of I am He, He is I, and I am I; let the distinctions remain open for careful reading.
shortened: Say: O people of the Bayan! Come, then tell Me truthfully: Who was it that spoke on Sinai to the Manifestation of the Revelation whom We named with Our name "He Who conversed with God" and sent unto him who disbelieved in God, the Lord of the Unseen and the Seen? If ye say the Tree spoke of its own accord, how then do ye deny this Call which hath been raised in truth? And if ye say He spoke in it, then He it is Who now speaketh: "There is no God but Me, the Forgiving, the Generous."

And in the station of "I am He," the Tree proclaimeth: "Verily, I am God, there is no God but Him, the Mighty, the Praised One." And in the station of "He is I," the Tongue of Grandeur speaketh among creation: "He is God, there is no God but Me, the All-Knowing, the All-Informed." And in the station of "Verily He is He," He speaketh and saith: "There is no God but Him, the Most High, the Most Great."

order.why: Keep the explicit rejection of self-extolling beside the claim that the purpose is God and His Cause.

I am the One Whom the tongue of Isaiah hath extolled, the One with Whose name both the Torah and the Evangel were adorned.

order.why: Let the relation of words to deeds enter the inquiry from the opening.
shortened: Say: God is My witness! I have wished nothing whatever for Myself. What I have wished is the victory of God and the triumph of His Cause. He is Himself a sufficient witness between you and Me. Were ye to cleanse your eyes, ye would readily perceive how my deeds testify to the truth of My words, how My words are a guide to My deeds.

order.why: Keep the preceding question and complete reported reply on Fatherhood, education and the mirror analogy.
shortened: Moreover as one of the perfect qualities of the Divinity is Fatherhood, therefore we give him the title of the Father; because the Manifestation of God is like unto a clear mirror in which is reflected the rays of the Sun of Reality and one of these rays is Fatherhood.

order.why: Preserve the full reported mirror analogy and its historical claims without converting the report into a canonical doctrinal formula.
shortened: The mirror of Jesus was entirely clear, so that it received the full light from the sun and was, therefore, the sun itself, and this was what Jesus meant when He said: "I and the Father are one."

In Tablets revealed by the Blessed Beauty there are also many such passages. The intent is an address from the Manifestation to Himself.

questions: How do the opening passages hold together the voice of divinity, the reception of revelation and the language of servitude? What changes when a declaration is read with its speaker, addressee and surrounding explanation?

What different relationships do the images of the Tree and its leaves, the Temple and its members, the Pen and the Book, or the ocean and its drops help us explore? Where might treating an image too literally obscure what the passage invites us to understand?

How do the claims of sovereignty sound when spoken from prison, exile or grief? What might these passages suggest about the relationship between spiritual authority, vulnerability and freedom from personal ambition?

How do the two comparative readings approach the relation between divine identity and human encounter? What light do Moses’ commission and the appeal to Jesus’ works cast on this compilation, and which differences call for further inquiry?

What happens when a universal declaration becomes a personal letter, a remembered visit or an answering prayer? How might the recurring acts of hearing, remembering and responding shape a reader’s own understanding of revelation?

Why do passages about divine speech lead into counsels on trustworthiness, friendship, wisdom, justice and the avoidance of strife? How could the connected subjects on the Holy Spirit, the stations of the Manifestation and divine sovereignty deepen an exploration of the relationship between recognition and action?

references.label: 1 · Exodus 3:1–15 · A voice, a name and a summons
references.note: Read the whole encounter at the burning bush in the King James Version. Attend to the distinction between the bush, the voice and Moses, and to the movement from holy ground and the divine name to a commission concerning an oppressed people. Compare this scene with the repeated appeal to Sinai in the compilation. What does the image of a speaking Tree make possible as a way of understanding revelation? How do the disclosure of identity, the hearer’s hesitation and a call to action belong together? Keep the biblical narrative’s particular setting in view while considering the Bahá’í texts’ use of its imagery.

references.label: 2 · John 14:7–11 · Seeing, speaking and the works
references.note: Read Philip’s request and Jesus’ reply in the King James Version. The passage connects seeing Jesus with seeing the Father, speaks of reciprocal indwelling, and directs attention to words and works. Set it beside this guide’s opening distinction between personal desire and divine speech, and beside the passages about servitude and the different stations of the Manifestation. How does each text connect the visible person with the divine source of revelation? What part do actions play in recognition? Compare the relationships expressed in these passages without assuming that Christian and Bahá’í accounts of Christ or revelation are identical.
